findings.title: New order() method is abstract and breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is an extensible interface, but order() was added as an abstract method instead of a default method. Any CryptoProvider implementation compiled against an earlier Keycloak version will throw AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration calls order() during sorting, and source code for such implementations will no longer compile. Adding a default implementation (for example returning a neutral order) would preserve compatibility while allowing built-in providers to override it.

findings.title: Equal-order providers are selected silently and nondeterministically
findings.body: detectProvider() now sorts only by order() and silently ignores every provider after the first, replacing the previous fail-fast error for multiple providers. DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, and WildFlyElytronProvider all return order 200, so if more than one is on the classpath the winner depends on ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order rather than configuration. In particular a non-FIPS provider could be selected where FIPS operation is required, silently weakening the intended security posture.

findings.title: AuthzClient installs the stub crypto provider as a global first-wins singleton
findings.body: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) calls CryptoIntegration.init(), and CryptoIntegration only initializes its static cryptoProvider once. When no higher-order provider is present this permanently installs AuthzClientCryptoProvider for the whole JVM, but that provider throws UnsupportedOperationException for PemUtils, CertificateUtils, signatures, ciphers, key factories, EC parameters, and most other CryptoProvider operations; a later attempt to initialize a full provider such as DefaultCryptoProvider will be ignored because the static provider is already set. Authz-client features or other Keycloak client code in the same process that need those operations will therefore fail unexpectedly.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an unrelated JCA provider
findings.body: The CryptoProvider contract for getBouncyCastleProvider() is to return the BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) provider, but this implementation returns the provider of the JVM default KeyStore type (typically SUN or SunJSSE). Callers that use the returned provider by name or for BouncyCastle-specific algorithms/services will fail or behave as if BouncyCastle were available when it is not. The Elytron provider already establishes the pattern of returning null when no BouncyCastle provider exists; returning an unrelated provider is more misleading and error-prone.

findings.title: ECDSA test uses one P-256 key for all curves and never verifies the converted signature
findings.body: The test generates a single default EC key pair (P-256 on standard JDKs) and then uses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512, and only asserts that DER-to-RS followed by RS-to-DER and back returns the same bytes. A self-consistent round trip can pass even if the DER output is not acceptable to a real verifier or if R/S padding/length handling for P-384 and P-521 is wrong. The test should generate a key pair on the curve matching each algorithm and verify that a signature converted to ASN.1 DER verifies with the JDK Signature object (and vice versa).
